newsitem.title: LEBANON: Solidere GDRs seek non-Arab finance for Beirut.
newsitem.headline: Solidere GDRs seek non-Arab finance for Beirut.

text.p: Solidere, the $2 billion real estate company which is rebuilding Beirut, on Tuesday offered non-Arabs their first chance of investing in the reconstruction of Lebanon's capital city.

Market sources in Beirut said Solidere began marketing Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) worth an expected $115-125 million, effectively giving non-Arabs the right to invest in Lebanon's biggest company.
"They launched an offer of GDRs today. They are making an international offering of 10 million GDRs for an issue size of $125 million," a source told Reuters.
The planned issue date was November 26, he said.
A Solidere executive questioned by Reuters about the planned issue declined to comment.
The 25-year Solidere project, launched in 1994, is the flagship of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's multi-billion-dollar drive to rebuild Lebanon from the ruins of the 1975-90 civil war.
The company calls it the world's biggest urban redevelopment project of the decade.
But non-Arab investors have until now been unable to participate since Lebanese law bars them from buying real estate in the country.
Solidere's heavily-oversubscribed $650 million share flotation in January 1994 was restricted to Lebanese and Arab investors.

GDRs are receipts which can be readily traded abroad, avoiding the registration complications of trading the underlying shares which they represent. However because of ownership restrictions, the Solidere GDRs would represent an economic interest in the underlying shares, rather than the shares themselves, the sources said.
Each GDR would be worth one-tenth of one of Solidere's shares. The company's A and B shares traded on the Beirut Stock Exchange on Tuesday at $114 and $117.75.
The price range on the GDRs was $11.5 to $12.5 for an issue price of $115-$125 million, the sources said.

The issue is lead managed by Merrill Lynch International, with a selling syndicate formed by ING Barings, Robert Fleming and Co, Paribas Capital Markets and UBS Ltd and roadshows will take place in the United States, Europe and elsewhere, a source said.

Solidere began work on rebuilding Beirut's war-shattered city centre -- an area covering 1.6 million square metres (400 acres) -- in late 1994. It plans to develop 4.4 million square metres (1,100 acres) of floor space.

Huge swathes of war-damaged buildings have been demolished and much of the infrastructure work has been done, and a number of buildings of architectural value have already been restored or are under restoration.
